title: OWASP Database Security Cheat Sheet
subcategory: Database hardening, authentication, least privilege, credential storage
core_concepts: application account must not own the database
credentials outside source code and repos
OS and DBMS hardening per CIS Benchmarks
engineering_principles: Treat the database as a protected backend reachable only through an API tier; require authentication everywhere; grant the application account only SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE and never ownership or instance-admin rights; keep credentials in protected configuration outside the web root and outside version control; for security-critical systems use table-, column- and row-level permissions or restricted views; remove default accounts/sample databases; patch; run the service as a low-privileged OS user.
practical_examples: Disable TCP in favour of local socket/localhost binding; SQL Server: disable xp_cmdshell, xp_dirtree, CLR, SQL Browser, Mixed Mode; MySQL: run mysql_secure_installation and disable the FILE privilege; store transaction logs on a separate disk; prefer Windows Integrated Authentication so no credential is stored.
why_it_matters: Defines the baseline role model (app role vs owner/migration role vs admin) and environment separation that every schema deployment pipeline should enforce; the 'account should not be the owner' rule is the direct justification for separating a DDL migration role from the runtime DML role.
authority_rationale: OWASP is the recognized community standards body for application security; cheat sheets are consensus guidance but not a formal standard and carry no revision date.
notes: Page shows no last-updated date. At-rest encryption guidance is thin (backups 'ideally encrypted'); defers PostgreSQL/MongoDB specifics to vendor docs.

title: OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
subcategory: Injection prevention
core_concepts: stored procedures are not inherently safe
allow-list validation for structural SQL elements
engineering_principles: 'Prepared statements treat bound values as data rather than SQL syntax.' Table/column names and sort direction cannot be bound and must be fixed in code or mapped from an allow-list. 'Do not use manual escaping as a substitute for parameter binding.' Least privilege 'does not prevent SQL injection' but limits blast radius; 'DO NOT ASSIGN DBA OR ADMIN TYPE ACCESS TO YOUR APPLICATION ACCOUNTS.' 'Validation of a value does not make it safe to concatenate into SQL.'
practical_examples: Bind every user-influenced value; parameterize dynamic SQL inside stored procedures; map a user's 'sort by' selection to one of a small set of application-owned column tokens; expose restricted views rather than base tables to the app account.
why_it_matters: Pipeline and migration code that builds SQL dynamically (e.g., per-tenant table names, generated DDL) is the schema-level injection surface; this sheet prescribes allow-listing structural identifiers and binding all values.
authority_rationale: OWASP consensus guidance; widely referenced by regulators and vendors, but community-maintained and undated.
notes: Companion: OWASP Query Parameterization Cheat Sheet (SEC-03).

title: OWASP Query Parameterization Cheat Sheet
subcategory: Parameterized queries by language/driver
core_concepts: bind variables in dynamic SQL within stored procedures
engineering_principles: 'SQL Injection is best prevented through the use of parameterized queries'; 'ensure that query parameterization is done server-side!' because client libraries may concatenate; 'Dynamic SQL can be parameterized using bind variables, to ensure the dynamically constructed SQL is secure.'
practical_examples: Java JDBC PreparedStatement and JPA/Hibernate named queries; .NET SqlCommand/SqlParameter; Ruby ActiveRecord; PHP PDO bindParam; ColdFusion cfqueryparam; Perl DBI; Rust SQLx; Oracle PL/SQL EXECUTE IMMEDIATE ... USING; SQL Server sp_executesql with named parameters.
why_it_matters: Gives the concrete API patterns data-engineering code (ETL, migration scripts, stored procedures) must use; especially relevant to procedures that construct DDL/DML strings.
authority_rationale: OWASP consensus guidance, undated.
notes: Page does not discuss parameterizing identifiers; see SEC-02 for that caveat.

title: OWASP Cryptographic Storage Cheat Sheet
subcategory: Encryption placement, algorithms, key management, key storage
core_concepts: encrypt at application/database/filesystem/hardware layer per threat model
do not store sensitive data if avoidable
no ECB; RSA >=2048 with OAEP; ML-KEM hybrid for PQ
formal key lifecycle and rotation triggers (cites SP 800-57 cryptoperiods)
keys stored separately from data (HSM/KMS/secrets manager)
no keys in code, VCS or environment variables
engineering_principles: 'Which layer(s) are most appropriate will depend on the threat model'; hardware/disk encryption does nothing against remote compromise. 'The best way to protect sensitive information is to not store it in the first place.' 'Where available, authenticated modes should always be used.' Rotate on compromise, cryptoperiod expiry, mode usage limits, or algorithm weakening; either re-encrypt or tag each record with its key ID and keep old keys for backups. Separate keys from data so one foothold (SQLi or traversal) cannot reach both.
practical_examples: SQL Server TDE as database-layer example; BitLocker/LUKS at filesystem; AWS KMS/Azure Key Vault/HashiCorp Vault for key storage; KEK derived from passphrase via KDF so passphrase change avoids re-encryption; language table of CSPRNG APIs (Java SecureRandom, Python secrets, Go crypto/rand, Node crypto.randomBytes).
why_it_matters: Supplies the decision framework for column-level vs TDE vs application-layer encryption and the key-ID-per-record pattern that enables key rotation and per-subject key destruction (crypto-shredding) in schema design.
authority_rationale: OWASP consensus guidance that cites NIST SP 800-57 and FIPS; undated.
notes: Does not cover column-level encryption or TDE limitations in detail; see SEC-23/SEC-24.

title: OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet
subcategory: Security event logging, data exclusion, log protection, retention
core_concepts: log authentication/authorization events, privilege and admin actions, sensitive-data access, key use
exclude passwords, tokens, keys, connection strings, session IDs, PII, cardholder data
structured (JSON) formats to prevent log injection
separate write-only database account for logs
engineering_principles: 'Build in tamper detection so you know if a record has been modified or deleted'; 'Store or copy log data to read-only media as soon as possible'; log data 'must not be destroyed before the duration of the required data retention period' nor kept beyond it; 'When using a database, it is preferable to utilize a separate database account that is only used for writing log data'; 'Do not use unstructured text log formats.'
practical_examples: Syslog over TLS to a central SIEM; hash session identifiers if tracking is needed; pseudonymize identities in logs; parameterized log templates in Java rather than concatenation.
why_it_matters: Defines what an audit/log table should and should not contain and establishes the write-only logging role and pseudonymous subject references that reconcile immutable logs with erasure rights.
authority_rationale: OWASP consensus guidance; undated.

title: OWASP Top 10:2025
subcategory: Top 10 web application risks, 2025 edition
publication_date: 2025 (exact release date not shown on page)
core_concepts: A08 Software or Data Integrity Failures
A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures
engineering_principles: Injection 'falls two spots from #3 to #5 in the ranking'; Cryptographic Failures 'falls two spots from #2 to #4'; Software Supply Chain Failures 'is an expansion of A06:2021-Vulnerable and Outdated Components'; Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions is 'a new category for 2025'. Data from 'over 2.8 millions applications', 589 CWEs (248 mapped), two categories from community survey.
practical_examples: Mapping schema controls to categories: RLS/least privilege -> A01; TDE/column encryption/key management -> A04; parameter binding -> A05; audit logging -> A09; fail-closed defaults in policy functions -> A10.
why_it_matters: Confirms the 2025 edition supersedes 2021 and that injection, cryptographic failures, access control and logging failures remain top risks that schema-level controls address.
authority_rationale: OWASP flagship awareness document widely referenced by PCI DSS and vendors; data-driven but community-produced; no release date on page.
notes: owasp.org/Top10/ redirects (308) to top10.owasp.org which redirects to the 2025 edition. Introduction page https://top10.owasp.org/2025/0x00_2025-Introduction also opened.

title: OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS) 5.0.0
subcategory: V14 Data Protection, V1.2 Injection Prevention, V11 Cryptography, V16 Logging
core_concepts: V14.1.1 identify and classify all sensitive data
V14.1.2 documented protection requirements per data level incl. database encryption, retention, logging
V14.2.6 return minimum sensitive data (e.g., partial card number)
V14.2.7 retention classification and automatic deletion
engineering_principles: Verify 'all sensitive data created and processed by the application has been identified' and classified; 'all sensitive data protection levels have a documented set of protection requirements' covering encryption, integrity, retention, logging, log access, database encryption and privacy controls; sensitive information 'is subject to data retention classification' with scheduled deletion.
practical_examples: Maintain a data inventory keyed to columns/fields with a protection level; drive column encryption, masking, retention jobs and log redaction from that classification; cite requirements as v5.0.0-14.1.1.
why_it_matters: Provides the verifiable requirement that schema metadata must carry a data classification and that retention/erasure is a designed property, not an afterthought.
authority_rationale: OWASP's formal verification standard, versioned and dated; community-developed rather than a national/international standard.
notes: Chapter list verified at https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/tree/v5.0.0/5.0/en; V14 requirement text from https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/blob/v5.0.0/5.0/en/0x23-V14-Data-Protection.md. V11 and V16 text not opened.

title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations
subcategory: AC, AU, SC, MP, PM, PT, SI control families
core_concepts: SC-28 Protection of Information at Rest
PM-25 Minimization of PII Used in Testing
engineering_principles: AC-3: 'Enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources'; AC-6: least privilege for users and processes; AU-9: 'Protect audit information and audit logging tools from unauthorized access, modification, and deletion'; AU-11: retain audit records for an organization-defined period 'to meet regulatory and organizational information retention requirements'; SC-28: protect confidentiality/integrity of information at rest including 'databases'; MP-6: sanitize media commensurate with classification; PM-25: 'Limit or minimize the amount of personally identifiable information used for internal testing, training, and research purposes.'
practical_examples: Map RLS/grants to AC-3/AC-6, pgAudit/SQL Server Audit to AU-2/AU-9/AU-11, TDE/column encryption to SC-28, KMS/HSM to SC-12, crypto-erase to MP-6, non-prod masking to PM-25, retention policies to SI-12.
why_it_matters: The canonical control vocabulary that regulators (HIPAA, FedRAMP) and auditors map to; gives named controls for each schema-security decision.
authority_rationale: US national standards body publication; mandatory for federal systems and the de facto reference control catalog globally.
notes: Landing page opened; control statements extracted locally via pdftotext from the official PDF https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-53r5.pdf (Sept 2020, 492 pp.). Release 5.2.0 changes not reviewed.

title: NIST SP 800-122: Guide to Protecting the Confidentiality of Personally Identifiable Information (PII)
organization_author: NIST (Erika McCallister, Tim Grance, Karen Scarfone)
subcategory: PII definition, confidentiality impact levels, de-identification, safeguards
core_concepts: PII definition (distinguish/trace identity; linked or linkable)
PII confidentiality impact level low/moderate/high distinct from FIPS 199
six factors: identifiability, quantity, data field sensitivity, context of use, obligation to protect, access/location
minimize use, collection and retention of PII (incl. SSNs)
re-identification key kept in a separate system
engineering_principles: 'PII is any information about an individual maintained by an agency, including (1) any information that can be used to distinguish or trace an individual's identity ... and (2) any other information that is linked or linkable to an individual.' 'Organizations should categorize their PII by the PII confidentiality impact level.' Quantity 'should only be raised and not lowered' the level. De-identified data can be rated low only if 'The re-identification algorithm, code, or pseudonym is maintained in a separate system, with appropriate controls.' Test PII 'is required to be protected at the same level that it is protected in the production' environment.
practical_examples: Impact-level examples: incident response roster (low), intranet tracking, fraud/waste/abuse reporting application (high); same name/address fields rated differently for a newsletter list vs undercover officers; plan to eliminate unnecessary SSN collection.
why_it_matters: Provides the classification scheme (impact level per data field and per context) and the architectural rule that pseudonym/key maps live in a separate system - the foundation for PII-separated schemas and tag-driven controls.
authority_rationale: NIST Special Publication; still the referenced federal PII guidance though dated 2010.
notes: Body text extracted locally from the official PDF https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-122.pdf. Definition of de-identification is 'loosely based on' the HIPAA Privacy Rule.

title: NIST SP 800-188: De-Identifying Government Datasets: Techniques and Governance
subcategory: De-identification techniques, re-identification risk, governance
engineering_principles: Define goals and assess release risk first; 'Agencies can create a Disclosure Review Board to oversee the process of de-identification'; adopt 'a de-identification standard with measurable performance levels and perform re-identification studies'; 'not all tools that merely mask personal information provide sufficient functionality for performing de-identification.'
practical_examples: Publishing synthetic data generated from identified data as one sharing model; transforming quasi-identifiers (dates, ZIP codes) before analytic release.
why_it_matters: Warns that column masking is not de-identification; analytic/data-warehouse schemas that claim anonymization must handle quasi-identifiers and measure re-identification risk.
authority_rationale: NIST Special Publication (final), 2023.
notes: Only the abstract/landing page was opened; technique details are from the abstract and keywords.

title: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5: Recommendation for Key Management, Part 1 - General
subcategory: Key lifecycle, cryptoperiods, security strength
engineering_principles: 'A cryptoperiod is the time span during which a specific key is authorized for use by legitimate entities or the keys for a given system will remain in effect.' A suitably defined cryptoperiod 'Limits the amount of information that is available for cryptanalysis', 'Limits the amount of exposure if a single key is compromised', limits algorithm lifetime, limits time for attacks on key protection, and 'Limits the time available for computationally intensive cryptanalysis.'
practical_examples: Define cryptoperiods for column-encryption keys and KEKs; store key IDs with encrypted records so rotation does not require simultaneous re-encryption; apply split knowledge for master keys.
why_it_matters: OWASP's rotation guidance defers to this document; any schema with encrypted columns or per-tenant/per-subject keys needs a cryptoperiod and rotation design.
authority_rationale: NIST Special Publication; referenced by FIPS 140-3 and PCI DSS key-management requirements.
notes: Landing page opened; cryptoperiod text extracted locally from the official PDF https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-57pt1r5.pdf. Related: FIPS 140-3 https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/140-3/final (opened; March 22, 2019; four security levels, aligned with ISO/IEC 19790).

title: NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2: Guidelines for Media Sanitization
organization_author: NIST (Ramaswamy Chandramouli) and Samsung Semiconductor (Eric Hibbard)
subcategory: Cryptographic erase (CE) as a purge technique
core_concepts: cryptographic erase = sanitization of encryption keys
CE preconditions: no prior plaintext storage
CE not trusted if keys backed up or escrowed without control
CE may be the only purge option for cloud/virtual storage
engineering_principles: 'At a basic level, CE is based on the sanitization of keys used to encrypt data or to prevent access to the keys that encrypt data. Thus, with CE, sanitization can be performed with high assurance much faster than with other sanitization techniques.' 'As a pre-condition for using CE, ISO/IEC 27040 specifies that no sensitive data has previously been stored on the ISM in plaintext form.' 'Sanitization using CE should not be trusted on ISM that have been backed up or escrowed unless the organization has a high level of confidence regarding how and where the keys were stored and managed.'
practical_examples: Self-encrypting drives with sanitize commands; cloud storage where CE 'may be the only viable purge sanitization technique option'; record CE operations in the sanitization program.
why_it_matters: The standards basis for crypto-shredding designs (per-subject or per-tenant keys destroyed to satisfy erasure while immutable logs remain): it legitimizes key destruction as erasure but imposes the conditions (encrypt from first write, control key backups, log the CE) a schema and key-management design must meet.
authority_rationale: NIST Special Publication (final, 2025) superseding Rev. 1 (2014).
notes: Landing page opened; CE text extracted locally from the official PDF https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-88r2.pdf. The document addresses storage media; applying CE to logical records inside a database is an engineering inference.

title: NIST Privacy Framework (Version 1.0; Version 1.1 Initial Public Draft)
subcategory: Core functions Identify-P, Govern-P, Control-P, Communicate-P, Protect-P
publication_date: v1.0 2020-01-16; v1.1 IPD 2025-04-14 (per NIST search results)
core_concepts: voluntary enterprise privacy risk management tool
1.1 realigns with CSF 2.0 and adds AI/privacy
engineering_principles: 'A voluntary tool developed in collaboration with stakeholders intended to help organizations identify and manage privacy risk.' 'The five Functions, Identify-P, Govern-P, Control-P, Communicate-P, and Protect-P ... can be used to manage privacy risks arising from data processing'; 'The Protect-P Function covers data protection to prevent cybersecurity-related privacy events.'
practical_examples: Use Identify-P data inventory and mapping outcomes to populate a data catalog with classifications; use Control-P outcomes for data minimization and de-identification controls in pipelines.
why_it_matters: Frames data inventory/mapping and data-processing controls as organizational outcomes that catalog tagging and schema classification implement.
authority_rationale: NIST framework document; voluntary.
notes: Functions text extracted locally from the official v1.0 PDF https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/CSWP/NIST.CSWP.01162020.pdf. 1.1 IPD details come from NIST search results (https://www.nist.gov/privacy-framework/new-projects/privacy-framework-version-11, https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/cswp/40/nist-privacy-framework-11/ipd) - not opened; final 1.1 publication not confirmed.

title: CIS Benchmarks (database benchmarks index)
subcategory: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle Database, MongoDB, MariaDB, Db2, Cassandra, Snowflake, cloud database services
core_concepts: archived older versions on CIS WorkBench
engineering_principles: 'The CIS Benchmarks are prescriptive configuration recommendations for more than 25+ vendor product families' that 'represent the consensus-based effort of cybersecurity experts globally.'
practical_examples: Listed: PostgreSQL 18 v1.0.0, 17 v1.1.0, 16 v1.1.0, 15 v1.2.0, 14 v1.3.0, 13 v1.4.0; Oracle MySQL 9.7 v1.0.0, 8.4 v1.1.0, 8.0 Enterprise v1.5.0/Community v1.2.0; Microsoft SQL Server 2025 v1.0.0, 2022 v1.3.0, 2019 v1.6.0; Oracle Database 26ai v1.0.0, 23ai v1.1.0, 19c v2.0.0; MongoDB 8 v2.0.0, 7 v2.0.0; MariaDB 10.11 v1.0.1; Snowflake Foundations v2.0.1; AWS Database Services v2.0.0; Microsoft Azure Database Services v2.0.0.
why_it_matters: OWASP points to CIS Benchmarks as the hardening baseline; pinning the benchmark version next to the engine version in migration/platform tooling makes hardening auditable.
authority_rationale: CIS is the recognized publisher of consensus hardening benchmarks referenced by PCI DSS and OWASP; official index page.
notes: Benchmark PDFs (with installation/logging/access-control/encryption sections and Level 1/Level 2 profiles) are registration-gated and were not opened; do not cite specific recommendation numbers.

title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (General Data Protection Regulation)
organization_author: European Parliament and Council of the European Union (EUR-Lex)
core_concepts: right to erasure and its legal-obligation/legal-claims exceptions
data protection by design and by default
security of processing incl. pseudonymisation and encryption
engineering_principles: Art. 5(1)(c): 'adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary'; 5(1)(e): 'kept in a form which permits identification of data subjects for no longer than is necessary'; Art. 17(3): erasure does not apply where processing is necessary 'for compliance with a legal obligation' or 'for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims'; Art. 25(1): measures 'such as pseudonymisation' designed to implement 'data minimisation'; 25(2): by default 'only personal data which are necessary for each specific purpose of the processing are processed'; Art. 32(1)(a): 'the pseudonymisation and encryption of personal data'; Recital 26: principles 'should therefore not apply to anonymous information'.
practical_examples: Model retention basis per table/column class to invoke Art. 17(3)(b)/(e) defensibly; keep pseudonym key maps separate (Art. 4(5)); record processing purposes and erasure time limits (Art. 30) alongside the schema catalog.
why_it_matters: Primary legal source for minimisation, pseudonymisation, erasure and the statutory resolution of the erasure-vs-retention conflict.
authority_rationale: Official EU legal text on EUR-Lex.
notes: Page text is ~380k characters; Articles 4, 5, 17, 25, 30, 32 and Recital 26 were read via offsets 0-300000. Exact Art. 17(1)(a)-(f) grounds were paraphrased by the fetch tool rather than quoted.

title: EDPB Guidelines 01/2025 on Pseudonymisation (version for public consultation)
subcategory: Pseudonymisation under Art. 4(5), 25, 32
core_concepts: lookup tables and cryptographic keys as additional information
technical and organisational measures preventing attribution
engineering_principles: Additional information 'may consist of tables matching pseudonyms with the identifying attributes they replace. It may also consist of cryptographic keys. Additional information kept by a pseudonymising controller or processor must be subject to technical and organisational measures ... In particular, the additional information is not to be disclosed to or used by persons processing the pseudonymised data. Such additional information may itself be personal data and so also subject to the GDPR.' The pseudonymisation domain 'may be restricted to defined' contexts and its effectiveness depends on 'its isolation from additional information.'
practical_examples: Separate identity/key schema with its own access roles; analytic tables carry only pseudonyms; the key table is itself classified as personal data.
why_it_matters: Authoritative EU interpretation that PII-separated schemas and per-subject key stores must be access-isolated from the teams/systems using pseudonymised data.
authority_rationale: EU regulator body guidance; however this is the public-consultation version and a final adopted text was not confirmed.
notes: Consultation landing page opened; guideline text extracted locally from the official PDF https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2025-01/edpb_guidelines_202501_pseudonymisation_en.pdf (URL returned verbatim by WebSearch; downloaded via curl).

title: PCI DSS v4.0.1 (PCI SSC announcement) with requirement text from PCI DSS v4.0 SAQ D for Merchants
subcategory: Requirement 3 (protect stored account data), 6.5.x (no live PAN in pre-production), 10 (audit logs)
publication_date: v4.0.1 announced 2024-06-11; v4.0 SAQ D April 2022; future-dated requirements effective 2025-03-31
core_concepts: SAD never stored after authorization, even encrypted
PAN masked on display (BIN + last four)
PAN unreadable anywhere stored: one-way hash, truncation, index tokens, strong cryptography with key management
disk/partition-level encryption alone insufficient for PAN
hashed and truncated versions must not be correlatable
audit logs enabled for all components and cardholder data; capture individual user access
v4.0 retired 2024-12-31; v4.0.1 adds no requirements
engineering_principles: 'SAD is not retained after authorization, even if encrypted.' 'PAN is rendered unreadable anywhere it is stored by using any of the following approaches: One-way hashes based on strong cryptography of the entire PAN; Truncation ...; Index tokens; Strong cryptography with associated key-management processes and procedures.' 'If disk-level or partition-level encryption (rather than file-, column-, or field-level database encryption) is used' PAN must be 'also rendered unreadable via another mechanism.' 'Live PANs are not used in pre-production environments, except where those environments are included in the CDE.' 'Retain audit log history for at least 12 months, with at least the most recent three months immediately available for analysis.'
practical_examples: Schema: no CVV/track/PIN columns or log fields post-authorization; PAN column tokenized or encrypted at column/field level with keyed hash for lookups; separate storage of truncated and hashed forms with controls against correlation; non-prod loaded only with synthetic/masked PANs; append-only audit tables retained >=12 months.
why_it_matters: Most prescriptive regulator-style text on how a sensitive column may be stored and queried, and the explicit statement that TDE/disk encryption alone does not satisfy PAN protection.
authority_rationale: Official PCI SSC publications (blog announcement and official SAQ D document on listings.pcisecuritystandards.org).
notes: Requirement wording extracted locally from the official v4.0 SAQ D for Merchants PDF https://listings.pcisecuritystandards.org/documents/PCI-DSS-v4-0-SAQ-D-Merchant.pdf (URL returned verbatim by WebSearch; downloaded via curl). PCI SSC states v4.0.1 has 'no additional or deleted requirements', but clause numbering (e.g., 6.5.x) was not re-verified against v4.0.1. Landing page https://www.pcisecuritystandards.org/standards/pci-dss/ also opened.

title: HIPAA Security Rule - 45 CFR 164.312 Technical safeguards (with 2025 NPRM)
organization_author: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (codified in CFR; published by GPO govinfo)
subcategory: Access control, audit controls, integrity, authentication, transmission security
core_concepts: integrity and mechanism to authenticate ePHI (Addressable)
2025 NPRM: remove addressable/required distinction, require encryption of ePHI, MFA, asset inventory and network map
engineering_principles: 164.312(a)(1): allow access 'only to those persons or software programs that have been granted access rights'; (a)(2)(i): 'Assign a unique name and/or number'; (b): 'Implement hardware, software, and/or procedural mechanisms that record and examine activity in information systems that contain or use electronic protected health information'; (c)(1): protect ePHI 'from improper alteration or destruction'; (a)(2)(iv): 'Implement a mechanism to encrypt and decrypt electronic protected health information' (Addressable). NPRM: 'remove the distinction between addressable and required implementation specifications'; 'By expressly requiring regulated entities to encrypt ePHI, with limited exceptions'.
practical_examples: Per-user database identities or propagated user context (no shared anonymous app identity without SESSION_CONTEXT-style attribution); object-level audit of ePHI tables; integrity mechanisms (checksums/hash chains) on ePHI records; column or at-rest encryption with documented rationale.
why_it_matters: Audit controls and integrity are standards (not addressable) and therefore must be designed into ePHI schemas; encryption is currently addressable but proposed to become required.
authority_rationale: Official codified regulation text from the U.S. Government Publishing Office; NPRM is the official Federal Register text.
notes: hhs.gov and ecfr.gov returned HTTP 403 / anti-bot redirects; govinfo mirrors used. NPRM read at https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2025-01-06/html/2024-30983.htm (chunks 0-330k of ~1.05M chars); items such as 72-hour restoration and scan/pen-test cadence were not located in the chunks read. Final-rule status not verified.

title: Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-204)
core_concepts: management assessment and auditor attestation of internal control over financial reporting (404)
criminal penalties for altering or destroying records (18 U.S.C. 1519)
tampering with records in official proceedings (1102 / 18 U.S.C. 1512(c))
engineering_principles: Sec. 404(a): annual report must 'state the responsibility of management for establishing and maintaining an adequate internal control structure'; 404(b): auditor 'shall attest to, and report on, the assessment made by the management of the issuer'; 18 U.S.C. 1519: 'Whoever knowingly alters, destroys, mutilates, conceals, covers up, falsifies, or makes a false entry in any record ... shall be fined under this title, imprisoned not more than 20 years, or both'; 18 U.S.C. 1520(a)(1): 'shall maintain all audit or review workpapers for a period of 5 years'.
practical_examples: Append-only/immutable financial ledgers and audit trails; retention schedules of 5-7 years for audit-relevant records; change-control evidence for schema migrations affecting financial systems.
why_it_matters: Legal source for immutable audit trails and multi-year retention that must coexist with GDPR/CCPA deletion rights; Art. 17(3)(b) GDPR expressly yields to such legal obligations.
authority_rationale: Official statutory text from GPO.
notes: congress.gov returned HTTP 403; govinfo used. Text read via offsets 0-233k.

title: California Consumer Privacy Act / CPRA - CPPA FAQ and Regulations
subcategory: Consumer rights, personal and sensitive personal information, thresholds, regulations effective 2026-01-01
publication_date: n.d. (CPRA amendments effective 2023-01-01; CCPA regulations effective 2026-01-01)
core_concepts: right to know, delete (subject to exceptions), correct, opt-out of sale/sharing, limit sensitive PI, equal treatment
personal information = identifies, relates to, or could reasonably be linked to a consumer or household
sensitive PI (SSN, driver's license, precise geolocation, genetic, health)
thresholds: $26.625M revenue, 100,000 residents/households, 50% revenue from selling/sharing
Sept 2025 regulations on cybersecurity audits, risk assessments, ADMT
engineering_principles: 'Right to DELETE personal information businesses have collected from them (subject to some exceptions)'; 'Right to LIMIT the use and disclosure of sensitive personal information'; 'Personal information is information that identifies, relates to, or could reasonably be linked to a particular consumer' or household.
practical_examples: Flag sensitive-PI columns distinctly from ordinary PI to support 'limit use' requests; implement deletion workflows that propagate to service providers and respect documented exceptions.
why_it_matters: Requires schema-level identification of sensitive personal information and deletion capability analogous to GDPR Art. 17, with its own exception set.
authority_rationale: Official California regulator FAQ and regulations page; FAQ is a summary rather than statutory text.
notes: oag.ca.gov (ECONNREFUSED) and leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (HTTP 403) could not be opened; exact text of Civ. Code 1798.105 exceptions not captured. Regulations page https://cppa.ca.gov/regulations/ also opened (lists 'CCPA Regulations (Effective January 1, 2026)').

title: PostgreSQL 18 Documentation: Row Security Policies
subcategory: Row-level security
core_concepts: bypass by superuser, BYPASSRLS, table owner
READ COMMITTED race conditions in policy subqueries
engineering_principles: 'If no policy exists for the table, a default-deny policy is used'; 'Table owners normally bypass row security as well, though a table owner can choose to be subject to row security with ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY'; 'care must be taken when developing schemas and row level policies to avoid covert channel leaks of information through such referential integrity checks'; prefer policies that 'consider only the current values in the row' for performance.
practical_examples: CREATE POLICY account_managers ON accounts TO managers USING (manager = current_user); restrictive policy requiring local socket for admins; SELECT ... FOR SHARE in policy subqueries; SECURITY DEFINER lookup functions.
why_it_matters: Reference implementation of tenant/row isolation in open-source RDBMS; the bypass and covert-channel rules dictate role design (app role must not own tables, or FORCE RLS) and FK design in multi-tenant schemas.
authority_rationale: Official PostgreSQL documentation.
notes: The common current_setting('app.tenant_id') pattern is not shown on the official page.

title: Row-Level Security - SQL Server, Azure SQL, Fabric
subcategory: Row-level security, SESSION_CONTEXT multi-tenant pattern, side channels
core_concepts: CREATE SECURITY POLICY with inline table-valued functions
applies to dbo/db_owner but they can alter policies
separate schema and ALTER ANY SECURITY POLICY role
side-channel attacks via crafted queries and malicious policy managers
leaks via CDC, Change Tracking, DBCC SHOW_STATISTICS; indexed views disallowed; temporal history needs own predicate
engineering_principles: 'Security policies apply to all users, including dbo users in the database'; 'If high privileged users, such as sysadmin or db_owner, need to see all rows ... the security policy must be written to allow that'; 'It's highly recommended to create a separate schema for the RLS objects'; error-based inference example SELECT 1/(SALARY-100000); 'Change Data Capture (CDC) can leak entire rows that should be filtered'.
practical_examples: Middle-tier pattern: sp_set_session_context @key=N'UserId', @value=..., @read_only=1; predicate checks DATABASE_PRINCIPAL_ID() = DATABASE_PRINCIPAL_ID('AppUser') AND CAST(SESSION_CONTEXT(N'UserId') AS int) = @AppUserId; DENY UPDATE ON Sales(AppUserId) TO AppUser; block predicate AFTER INSERT.
why_it_matters: Shows how to implement tenant isolation when the app uses one database login, and enumerates schema features (CDC, change tracking, indexed views, temporal tables) that silently undermine RLS.
authority_rationale: Official Microsoft product documentation with revision date.
notes: Fabric and Synapse support filter predicates only.

title: Always Encrypted - SQL Server and Azure SQL
subcategory: Client-side column encryption; deterministic vs randomized; secure enclaves
core_concepts: separation of data owners from data managers (DBAs, cloud operators)
column encryption keys and column master keys in external key store
deterministic encryption enables equality, joins, grouping, indexing but leaks patterns
randomized encryption supports no operations without enclaves
secure enclaves add in-place encryption, pattern matching and range comparisons
engineering_principles: 'This approach provides a separation between those who own the data and can view it, and those who manage the data but should have no access: on-premises database administrators, cloud database operators, or other high-privileged unauthorized users.' 'Deterministic encryption always generates the same encrypted value ... you can perform point lookups, equality joins, grouping, and indexing ... However, unauthorized users might guess information about encrypted values by examining patterns.' 'The Database Engine doesn't store or use any keys in plaintext.'
practical_examples: Column master key in Azure Key Vault/HSM; deterministic encryption on SSN for equality lookups; randomized on free-text; unsupported: IDENTITY, computed, sparse, FILESTREAM, CHECK/DEFAULT constraints, randomized PK/FK/unique/index, CDC, DDM, non-_BIN2 collations; re-encryption performed outside the engine unless enclaves are used.
why_it_matters: Defines the real trade-off between confidentiality against insiders and schema expressiveness (indexes, constraints, query operators); the insider threat model it addresses is exactly what TDE does not cover.
authority_rationale: Official Microsoft product documentation with revision date.
notes: Compare SEC-24 (TDE) and SEC-25 (DDM); DDM cannot be applied to Always Encrypted columns.

title: Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) - SQL Server
subcategory: Encryption at rest; key hierarchy; limits
core_concepts: real-time page-level I/O encryption of data and log files
key hierarchy DPAPI -> SMK -> DMK -> certificate/EKM -> DEK
backups encrypted with DEK; certificate loss = data loss
FILESTREAM and buffer pool extension not encrypted
tempdb encrypted when any user DB is
engineering_principles: 'TDE protects data at rest, which is the data and log files'; protects against 'a malicious party who steals physical media like drives or backup tapes'; 'TDE doesn't provide encryption across communication channels'; 'Data loss results if the certificates are no longer available.' The page makes no claim of protection against authorized or privileged users querying the database.
practical_examples: CREATE DATABASE ENCRYPTION KEY WITH ALGORITHM = AES_256 ENCRYPTION BY SERVER CERTIFICATE ...; ALTER DATABASE ... SET ENCRYPTION ON; back up certificate and private key immediately; monitor via sys.dm_database_encryption_keys; audit TDE changes via DATABASE_OBJECT_CHANGE_GROUP.
why_it_matters: Source for the 'TDE marketing vs threat model' conflict: Microsoft itself scopes TDE to at-rest media theft, while PCI DSS 3.5.1.2 says disk/partition-level encryption alone is insufficient for PAN.
authority_rationale: Official Microsoft product documentation with revision date.
notes: Page states TDE 'lets you follow many laws, regulations, and guidelines' - a positioning statement that conflicts with PCI DSS 3.5.1.2 for PAN specifically.

title: Dynamic Data Masking - SQL Server
subcategory: Query-time masking; UNMASK permission; inference bypass
core_concepts: bypass by inference and brute force
SELECT INTO by non-UNMASK user yields statically masked copy
engineering_principles: 'Dynamic data masking doesn't aim to prevent database users from connecting directly to the database and running exhaustive queries that expose pieces of the sensitive data'; 'dynamic data masking shouldn't be used alone to fully secure sensitive data from users running ad hoc queries ... It's appropriate for preventing accidental sensitive data exposure, but doesn't protect against malicious intent'; 'always follow the minimal required permissions principle ... have Auditing enabled'.
practical_examples: Phone VARCHAR(12) MASKED WITH (FUNCTION = 'default()'); Email MASKED WITH (FUNCTION = 'email()'); GRANT UNMASK ON Data.Membership(FirstName) TO ServiceAttendant; inference example WHERE Salary > 99999 and Salary < 100001.
why_it_matters: Clarifies that masking is a presentation control for accidental exposure, not a confidentiality control; also offers a cheap way to produce statically masked non-production copies.
authority_rationale: Official Microsoft product documentation with revision date.
notes: Cannot mask Always Encrypted columns, FILESTREAM, computed columns, or columns in indexed views.

title: SQL Server Audit (Database Engine)
subcategory: Server/database audit specifications, targets, tamper resistance
core_concepts: server audit -> server audit specification + database audit specifications
audit action groups and object-level actions built on Extended Events
targets: file, Windows Security log, Application log
file ACL model for audit admins/readers
audit dbo to capture sysadmin actions
sysadmin can tamper with audit components
engineering_principles: 'Members of the sysadmin fixed server role are identified as the dbo user in each database. To audit actions of the administrators, audit the actions of the dbo user.' 'Principals in the sysadmin role can tamper with any audit component.' 'We recommend that you generate audit reports from a separate instance of SQL Server ... to which only Audit Administrators or Audit Readers have access.' 'Any authenticated user can read and write to the Windows Application event log ... less secure than the Windows Security event log.'
practical_examples: Create audit with file target on ACL-restricted/BitLocker folder; database audit specification on sensitive tables; define an audit on master.sys.fn_get_audit_file to record who reads the audit; all editions support database-level audit since SQL Server 2016 SP1.
why_it_matters: Implements PCI DSS Req. 10 / HIPAA audit controls at object level and documents the residual superuser-tampering risk that justifies shipping logs off-box.
authority_rationale: Official Microsoft product documentation with revision date.
notes: tempdb and temporary tables are not audited.

title: pgAudit - PostgreSQL Audit Extension
subcategory: Session and object audit logging for PostgreSQL
core_concepts: session audit logging by class: READ, WRITE, FUNCTION, ROLE, DDL, MISC, MISC_SET
logs what happened, not just what was requested
engineering_principles: 'The standard logging facility shows what the user requested, while pgAudit focuses on the details of what happened while the database was satisfying the request'; 'Audit logging is best-effort and not transactional'; 'not possible to reliably audit superusers with pgAudit'.
practical_examples: pgaudit.log = 'write, ddl, role'; pgaudit.role = 'auditor' with GRANT SELECT on sensitive tables to capture reads; CREATE TABLE inside a DO block is logged with its fully qualified name.
why_it_matters: The de facto compliance audit tool for PostgreSQL (open-source RLS counterpart to SQL Server Audit); its superuser limitation drives the need for non-superuser application roles.
authority_rationale: Official project repository/README of the widely adopted extension; not a standards body.
notes: Only superusers can change pgaudit settings; each major PostgreSQL version has its own branch.

title: Oracle Database 19c Security Guide: Introduction to Auditing (Unified Auditing)
subcategory: Unified audit trail, audit policies, AUDIT_ADMIN/AUDIT_VIEWER roles
core_concepts: mandatory audits that cannot be turned off
auditing of database and non-database (CLIENT_IDENTIFIER) users
engineering_principles: 'The unified audit trail table AUD$UNIFIED is a specialized table ... which allows only INSERT activity. Any attempt to directly truncate, delete or update contents of the AUD$UNIFIED table fail, and generate audit records.' 'Oracle Database has mandatory audits that cannot be turned off.' AUDIT_ADMIN: 'Grant this role only to trusted users.'
practical_examples: Check SELECT VALUE FROM V$OPTION WHERE PARAMETER = 'Unified Auditing'; grant AUDIT_VIEWER to external auditors; correlate INSERT failures with Database Vault realm violations in one trail.
why_it_matters: A vendor-implemented model of an append-only, tamper-evident audit store with segregated administrator/viewer roles - the pattern to emulate for application-level audit tables.
authority_rationale: Official Oracle product documentation.
notes: Page does not use the term 'tamper-evident'; INSERT-only behavior is the stated mechanism.

title: Oracle Database 2 Day + Security Guide 12.2: Restricting Access with Oracle Virtual Private Database
subcategory: Virtual Private Database (row/column-level policies)
core_concepts: dynamic WHERE clause appended to SQL
engineering_principles: 'Oracle Virtual Private Database (VPD) enables you to dynamically add a WHERE clause in any SQL statement that a user executes'; 'You create and manage the VPD policy at the database table or view level, which means that you do not modify the applications that access the database'; security in the database 'is present and enforced no matter how users (or intruders) try to access the data'.
practical_examples: Policy function returns '1=1' for sales reps and '1=2' otherwise using sys_context('userenv','session_user') joined to HR.EMPLOYEES; policy ACCESSCONTROL_ORDERS on OE.ORDERS, type CONTEXT_SENSITIVE, enforced on SELECT.
why_it_matters: Oracle's RLS equivalent; the fail-closed default predicate and context-sensitive evaluation are directly reusable design ideas for predicate-based isolation.
authority_rationale: Official Oracle documentation, though an older (12.2) tutorial guide; current 19c chapter TOC also opened.
notes: 19c chapter https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/19/dbseg/using-oracle-vpd-to-control-data-access.html opened (TOC only). EXEMPT ACCESS POLICY bypass and sec_relevant_cols details come from search snippets, not opened pages.

title: MongoDB Security Checklist
subcategory: Pre-production and production security checklist
core_concepts: enable access control and authentication (SCRAM, X.509, LDAP, Kerberos)
RBAC with least privilege and unique users per person/application
Client-Side Field Level Encryption / Queryable Encryption
periodic CVE review and credential rotation
engineering_principles: 'Create a unique MongoDB user for each person/application that accesses the system'; 'Follow the principle of least privilege'; encrypt fields 'application-side prior to transmitting data over the wire to the server'; 'Audit records permit forensic analysis and allow administrators to exercise proper controls'; 'Review MongoDB database users and periodically rotate them.'
practical_examples: net.bindIp, security.clusterIpSourceAllowlist, per-user authenticationRestrictions; --noscripting; exclude dbPath and log path from antivirus scanning.
why_it_matters: Document-database counterpart to the OWASP database checklist; CSFLE/Queryable Encryption are the NoSQL analogue of Always Encrypted for field-level protection against server-side insiders.
authority_rationale: Official MongoDB documentation.
notes: Auditing is an Enterprise/Atlas feature.

title: Snowflake Documentation: Object Tagging
subcategory: Tags, tag-based masking policies, classification, lineage
core_concepts: schema-level tag objects with string values
tag inheritance table -> columns and propagation to dependent objects
tag_admin role / centralized vs decentralized governance
engineering_principles: 'A tag is a schema-level object that can be assigned to another Snowflake object'; 'assign a masking policy to a tag, then assign that tag to a table or column' so 'the tagged column is automatically protected by the masking policy'; 'if a tag is set on a table, the tag will be inherited by all columns in that table'.
practical_examples: tag_admin custom role creates and applies PII tags; classification sets a tag automatically on columns detected as sensitive; TAG_REFERENCES_WITH_LINEAGE shows whether a tag was set manually, inherited or propagated.
why_it_matters: Makes PII classification machine-enforceable in the warehouse: the tag drives masking automatically, so schema-level classification and protection are coupled.
authority_rationale: Official Snowflake documentation.
notes: SEMANTIC_CATEGORY / PRIVACY_CATEGORY system-tag names were not visible on this page.

title: Databricks Unity Catalog: Apply tags to Unity Catalog securable objects
subcategory: Tags, governed tags, ABAC inheritance
core_concepts: tags on catalogs, schemas, tables, columns, volumes, views, functions, models
governed tags with enforced permissions and allowed values
ABAC: tags inherit down the object hierarchy (not to columns)
tag data is plain text and may be replicated globally
limits 50 tags per securable, 1,000 column tags per table
dropping a column with governed tags fails
engineering_principles: 'Governed tags are account-level tags with enforced rules for consistency and control'; 'tags applied at one level of the Unity Catalog object model automatically apply to all objects beneath it' for ABAC evaluation; 'Tag data is stored as plain text and may be replicated globally' - do not store sensitive values in tags.
practical_examples: Classification/ownership/lifecycle system tags; ABAC policies keyed on governed PII tags; column drop blocked until governed tags removed.
why_it_matters: Lakehouse analogue of Snowflake tagging: governed tags give a controlled PII vocabulary that policies consume, and the column-drop guard protects classification integrity during migrations.
authority_rationale: Official Databricks documentation.
notes: Row filters and column masks are documented on a separate page not opened.

title: BigQuery: Introduction to column-level access control (policy tags)
subcategory: Policy tag taxonomies, Fine-Grained Reader, dynamic masking
core_concepts: taxonomy of policy tags (up to five levels)
Fine-Grained Reader role required to read protected columns
enforcement at taxonomy level; works in addition to dataset ACLs
limits: 1,000 unique policy tags per table, no legacy SQL, regional taxonomies
engineering_principles: 'A policy tag hierarchy can be no more than five levels deep from the root node to the lowest-level subtag'; 'Enforcing access control causes the access restrictions defined for all of the policy tags in the taxonomy to be applied'; 'Data masking lets you mask sensitive data by substituting null, default, or hashed content in place of the column's actual value.'
practical_examples: Business-criticality taxonomy with High/Medium nodes; grant Fine-Grained Reader on the High tag; SELECT * EXCEPT (ssn) for users lacking the role.
why_it_matters: Shows column-level ACL implemented through catalog metadata rather than views, a pattern for separating PII access from table access in analytic schemas.
authority_rationale: Official Google Cloud documentation.
notes: cloud.google.com URL redirected (301) to docs.cloud.google.com; redirected page opened. Interaction with row-level security not described on this page.

title: Architectural approaches for storage and data in multitenant solutions (Azure Architecture Center)
organization_author: Microsoft Azure Patterns & Practices (John Downs et al.)
subcategory: Multitenant data isolation models, antipatterns, schema versioning
core_concepts: shared database vs database-per-tenant vs sharding vs deployment stamps vs geodes
isolate tenants needing own encryption keys, backup policies or geographies
antipatterns: table-per-tenant, column-level tenant customization, manual schema changes, single-version dependency
row-level security requires propagating tenant identity on every query
tenant-level encryption via Always Encrypted / customer-managed keys
engineering_principles: 'Instead, consider using a single set of multitenant tables with a tenant identifier column'; 'build tooling or an automated pipeline to deploy your schema changes ... Track the schema version that you use for each tenant'; 'ensure that your application version is backwards-compatible with at least one previous schema version, and sequence destructive schema changes across multiple versions to support rollbacks'; 'Many multitenant solutions don't use row-level security because of those complexities.'
practical_examples: Azure SQL elastic pools for database-per-tenant; Cosmos DB per-tenant containers; application tier detects schema version per tenant database and triggers upgrade; restore a single tenant from a shared database by restoring to a separate resource.
why_it_matters: Directly addresses secure multi-tenant schema design and secure migration practice (versioned, automated, backward-compatible, sequenced destructive changes) and gives a sober view of RLS operational cost.
authority_rationale: Official Microsoft architecture guidance (major-organization engineering guidance rather than product spec).

title: AWS Well-Architected SaaS Lens: Tenant Isolation (with SaaS Tenant Isolation Strategies whitepaper)
subcategory: Tenant isolation principles; silo/pool/bridge models
core_concepts: tenant isolation as a foundational SaaS requirement
isolation strategy depends on domain, compliance, deployment model and services
engineering_principles: 'Tenant isolation is one of the foundational topics that every SaaS provider must address ... Crossing this boundary in any form would represent a significant and potentially unrecoverable event for a SaaS business'; 'each SaaS architecture needs to ensure that it has put in place the constructs that are needed to ensure that each tenant's resources have been effectively isolated.'
practical_examples: Per the whitepaper (search results): silo = each tenant runs a fully siloed stack; pool = shared infrastructure where 'an outage will likely impact all the tenants'; bridge = pooled web tier with siloed business logic and storage; premium tiers run as silo clones of the pooled version.
why_it_matters: Frames tenant isolation as a non-negotiable architectural property to be enforced by platform constructs, not only application logic - the rationale for RLS/VPD, per-tenant databases or scoped credentials in data tiers.
authority_rationale: Official AWS Well-Architected guidance; the standalone whitepaper is marked for historical reference per search results.
notes: Whitepaper URLs https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/saas-tenant-isolation-strategies/core-isolation-concepts.html and .../the-bridge-model.html were returned verbatim by WebSearch; fetching the whitepaper URLs returned the SaaS Lens landing page content, so silo/pool/bridge wording relies on search snippets and the fetched SaaS Lens page.
